\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.39$\times$ latency).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.

3	At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
4	The final mask is their conjunction:
5	%
6	\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
7	  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
8	\end{equation}
9	%
10	where $\wedge$ denotes element-wise AND over the vocabulary $V$; a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
11	The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$. This reflects the scale-dependent layer interaction (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property enforced only by the grammar layer.
12	This dependency is scale-sensitive: 70B semantic-only achieves 84\% DR reduction (vs.\ 24\% on 8B), though grammar remains necessary for RV elimination (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
13	
14	\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
15	When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
16	We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
17	Structural integrity is a hard constraint; type violations are soft errors detectable by downstream validation, with DR (ontologically invalid type pair) more severe than CF (individually valid triples with cross-triple type inconsistency).
18	Extraction tasks are robust to format-level constraints~\cite{tam2024letmespeak}, supporting this asymmetric treatment.
19	
20	\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
21	\label{eq:tightness}
22	Per-relation constraint tightness $\kappa(r) = 1 - |\sigma(r)|/|\mathcal{E}|^2$ captures schema restrictiveness; DR reduction correlates descriptively with schema-mean $\bar{\kappa}$ across our three evaluation schemas ($n{=}3$), though entity type confusability is a significant co-factor (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa-case-study},~\ref{app:tcr}).
23	
24	\paragraph{Greedy limitation and fallback cascade.}
25	\label{sec:greedy-limitation}
26	Single-pass per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate type assignments across triples sharing the same entity mention; cross-field consistency requires global inference that exceeds the per-token masking paradigm.
27	The semantic layer commits entity types greedily---an instance of Level~3 (non-local) constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability})---so CF violations arise when the same entity receives different types across triples; beam search mitigates this (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
28	Fallback triggers on 0.5--5.7\% of type-bearing positions (zero-shot), virtually eliminated by fine-tuning ($\leq$\,0.11\%); all residual DR occurs at fallback positions (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}).
29	
30	\paragraph{Non-rectangularity and independent enforcement.}
31	\label{sec:rectangularity}

**C3 (Scale exploration)**: "Preliminary single-family... 84% vs 24% independent DR reduction"
- This is appropriately hedged and correctly scoped.

The paper has several underutilized findings: the 97.6-100% false positive rate among removed triples is massive but currently hidden in a parenthetical in §5, the zero-shot F1 improvements across multiple settings aren't highlighted in the abstract, and there are other data points that could strengthen the narrative if repositioned.

The narrative structure holds up well: the problem of invalid triples is clear, the gap in existing approaches is well-articulated, the two-layer method with decidability justification feels novel, and the non-additive composition finding (3% + 24% → 94%) anchors the results. The severity-weighted framing helps, but these are all angles where pushback could come.

There's also the missing piece—I haven't actually validated that the approach composes orthogonally with other constraint-handling methods like GoLLIE or OntoCoDec, just claimed it theoretically should.
